newsitem.title: UK: Dollar surges in Europe after French Socialist win.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges in Europe after French Socialist win.

text.p: The dollar powered to near four-week peaks against the mark and French franc in Europe, giddy after France's left-wing opposition swept to power in parliamentary elections on Sunday.
Analysts said the dollar would remain a darling on currency markets after French election results showed the Socialists would have to rely on the Communists to form a government.

Uncertainty over European Monetary Union, after Socialist leader and Prime Minister in-waiting Lionel Jospin said voters had demanded reorientation on Europe, will also boost the U.S. unit against European currencies.

At 0750 GMT dollar/mark was at 1.7133/38 against 1.7082/92 in late Europe on Friday, but just below near four-week peaks of 1.7170 marks hit earlier in Europe. Dollar/French franc was at 5.7930/50 against 5.7960/20 in late Europe, though just below early highs around 5.8132.
Against the yen, however, the dollar was little changed to a touch softer, trading at 116.17/6.27 yen against 116.37/47.

"It is the Socialists winning in a manner in which they will have to depend on the Communists, known EMU opponents, (that will boost the dollar),", said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase Investment Bank.

"This (the election) has been the straw that has broken the camel's back, as it raises further uncertainty about European issues - particularly those concerning EMU. That is why sterling and the dollar have done well over the last 24 hours," said Gunner.

Markets are closely watching France for any signs of EMU delay after Jospin said voters had demanded reorientation on Europe. The left-wing is expected to adopt a looser interpretation of the Maastricht treaty, paving the way for a softer euro at the outset, said analysts. A delay to EMU is also expected to buoy the mark, but a soft euro would depress it.

Victory for France's Socialists, seen as keen on Italy and Spain to be included among EMU's founding members, comes on the heels of the German government's plans to revalue Bundesbank assets in a bid to qualify for EMU. Both developments improve the odds of a broad-based EMU and a softer euro from the outset.

"The French election results have increased the prospect of a softer euro. That is clearly bad news for the deutschmark, and clearly the dollar has benefited," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
Francois Hollande, spokesman for the victorious Socialists, called for Italy and Spain to be included in EMU.
And said all stood to benefit if the euro "no longer means austerity."
But reports that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer had suggested delaying EMU's planned start in 1999, were firmly denied in a statement to Reuters by the Buba on Sunday.

"Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer makes the following statement about the current public discussion and some false reports: The Deutsche Bundesbank naturally stands by the Maastricht Treaty. The bank has already been working intensively for some time on the preparation of the monetary union with a stable euro."

It also said that "reports of suggestions by the Bundesbank or its president in favour of a postponment of the start of the monetary union are not accurate. According to the (Maastricht) treaty, the political decision over membership in the monetary union will only be made in early 1998."
